# Dereplication of plant phenolics using a mass-spectrometry database independent method

**Authors:** Ricardo M. Borges; Rahil Taujale; Juliana Santana de Souza; Thaís de Andrade Bezerra; Eder Lana e Silva; Ronny Herzog; Francesca V. Ponce; Jean-Luc Wolfender; Arthur S. Edison

**Affiliations:** 1Complex Carbohydrate Research Centre (CCRC), Departments of Genetics and Biochemistry, Institute of Bioinformatics, University of Georgia, Athens, GA, USA | 2Natural Product Research Institute Walter Mors (IPPN), Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ), Rio de Janeiro, Brazil | 3Lipotype GmbH, Dresden, Germany | 4School of Pharmaceutical Sciences, EPGL, University of Geneva, University of Lausanne, CMU, Geneva, Switzerland

## Abstract

Dereplication, an approach to sidestep the efforts involved in the isolation of known compounds, is generally accepted as being the first stage of novel discoveries in natural product research. It is based on metabolite profiling analysis of complex natural extracts.

To present the application of LipidXplorer for automatic targeted dereplication of phenolics in plant crude extracts based on direct infusion high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry data.

LipidXplorer uses a user-defined molecular fragmentation query language (MFQL) to search for specific characteristic fragmentation patterns in large data sets and highlight the corresponding metabolites. To this end, MFQL files were written to dereplicate common phenolics occurring in plant extracts. Complementary MFQL files were used for validation purposes.

New MFQL files with molecular formula restrictions for common classes of phenolic natural products were generated for the metabolite profiling of different representative crude plant extracts. This method was evaluated against an open-source software for mass-spectrometry data processing (MZMine®) and against manual annotation based on published data.

The targeted LipidXplorer method implemented using common phenolic fragmentation patterns, was found to be able to annotate more phenolics than MZMine® that is based on automated queries on the available databases. Additionally, screening for ascarosides, natural products with unrelated structures to plant phenolics collected from the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, demonstrated the specificity of this method by cross-testing both groups of chemicals in both plants and nematodes.

## INTRODUCTION

Direct infusion electrospray ionisation mass spectrometry (DI-ESI-MS) based dereplication allows a rapid and qualitative visualisation of the sample constituents in complex mixture in only a few minutes. But the sheer volume of data produced by such state of the art technology creates difficulties for the manual or automated annotation of groups of compounds of interest. To facilitate annotation, software and computational toolboxes have been developed and aid the interpretation of such convoluted data. MS2Analyser,1 MzMine,2 and XCMS,3 LipidBlast,4 LipidProfiler5 are some popular examples. However, such approaches all rely on a well-defined library6–8 and the natural product chemistry community still lacks a comprehensive open access database. Progress has recently been made to implement in silico tandem mass spectrometry (MS2) libraries to improve the process.9–11 Such approaches, however, are limited to classical dereplication only and cannot annotate unknown compounds or even classify them since those would not be part of any experimental database.

LipidXplorer is an open source Python language software kit to analyse MS-based lipidomic acquired data.6 This software is based on the declarative molecular fragmentation query language (MFQL), which allows users to input search parameters for their specific goals. Originally it was designed to support shotgun lipidomics profiling of multiple samples through the organisation of the acquired data into a flat-file database (the Masterscan file; *.sc), followed by filtering with selected user-defined MFQL files (*.mfql).8 The output file (MFQL files) includes the identification of the precursors, their fragments and abundance for subsequent quantification. The most important feature of LipidXplorer as an exploratory tool is the flexibility of programming of the MFQL files for either a given metabolite or a class of compounds sharing a similar fragmentation pattern. It is possible to submit a batch of samples to LipidXplorer to screen all samples and even obtain quantitative results depending on the experimental design.8

In this paper, a general method is described where LipidXplorer fragmentation pattern queries were designated for automatic dereplication of phenolics in medicinal plants using electrospray high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry data. Phenolic compounds were chosen since they are widely distributed in plants and other organisms. Their importance is closely related to their antioxidant properties. Many well-known biological activities such as antimicrobial, antitumor, and cardiovascular benefits are associated with the regular ingestion of phenolics.12–14

MFQL files with molecular structure restrictions were created for the main classes of phenolics and used for dereplication. The method was tested on well-studied plants extracts. In addition, the same strategy was applied to screen unrelated extracts from nematodes, which are expected to have fewer phenolic compounds, to test the specificity of the suggested method. MFQL files for ascarosides,15,16 a major family of pheromones in nematodes that are not found in plants, were also created.

## EXPERIMENTAL

### Reagents, plant and worm material

All plant material was collected from the State Botanical Garden of Georgia (Athens, GA, USA) (Table 1). An original sample of hesperidin was acquired from HWI Analytik GMBH and Acros Organics. Samples of Caenorhabditis elegans N2 strain were acquired from Caenorhabditis Genetics Centre (CGC; University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN) and were used to evaluate the versatility and the selectivity of the method proposed here (Table 1). HPLC grade methanol and LC-MS grade water was acquired from Fisher Scientific (Waltham, MA, USA).

### Sample preparation

Dried leaf material (30 mg) of each sample was ground and extracted with 80% methanol (1.5 mL) at room temperature using sonication. After three cycles of 8 min each, the extraction mixtures were centrifuged for 10 min at 10000×g at 4°C. The supernatants were filtered and concentrated under vacuum. This procedure was repeated twice for each sample for maximum recovery, and the final solution was concentrated to dryness. The original sample of hesperidin (C28H34O15) was acquired from Sigma-Aldrich (St Louis, MO, USA) and the solution was prepared at 80% methanol (1 mg/mL) at room temperature using sonication. After three cycles of 8 min each, the extraction mixtures were centrifuged for 10 min at 10000×g at 4°C, and the supernatants were kept for analysis after resuspension in 50% methanol (1 mL).

The Caenorhabditis elegans samples were produced as described elsewhere.17,18 A single L1 animal was placed in a 10 cm nematode growth media (NGM)17 seeded plate and left for 9 days to grow and reproduce. Worms were then washed off the plate using M9 Buffer17 and transferred to a 15 mL centrifuge tube. To remove bacteria left over in the plate, worms were centrifuged for 2 min at 2000 rpm and washed three times using the buffer solution. Then, 15000 young larvae were suspended in 2 mL of S-complete,17 placed in a 50 mL Erlenmeyer flask and fed 250 μL of Escherichia coli. The cultures were then allowed to shake at 22 °C until they reached adult stage (~55 h). To achieve a synchronous population of worms, eggs were collected by treating adult worms with a bleach solution. Eggs were then hatched at 22 °C in the buffer. After 24 h, L1 larvae were washed and counted. An aliquot containing 30000 worms was placed in a 50 mL Erlenmeyer flask with S-complete (4 mL),17 fed 400 μL of Escherichia coli, and allowed to shake at 22°C until they reached young adult stage (~42 h). Once the worms reached young adult stage, they were pelleted by centrifugation. The supernatant was collected, centrifuged, and immediately frozen at −80 °C. A sucrose gradient was used to separate the worms from the residual bacteria in the culture before collection of the worm samples. All samples were washed and immediately frozen at −80 °C. The supernatant was then centrifuged at high speed, lyophilised, and resuspended in 80% methanol (1 mL).18 The worm bodies were homogenised in a FastPrep-24 MP using 80% methanol and a lysing matrix and centrifuged. The supernatant was collected and then dried using a speedvac. Residues were resuspended in 50% methanol (1 mL) for analysis.18

### Electrospray mass spectrometry analysis

Full-scan ESI-MS analysis were performed using an Orbitrap Fusion mass spectrometer (Thermo, Waltham, MA, USA), at a resolution of 400000 at m/z 200, equipped with a nano-electrospray interface EASY-Spray™ (ThermoFischer Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). Samples were infused directly into the source at a flow rate of 0.5 μL/min. The ion transfer tube temperature was set at 325°C. Data were acquired in negative mode in the range m/z 150–1500 and the capillary voltage was set to 1.5 kV. Since phenolics are acidic compounds, they are more sensitive to negative mode ionisation. MS2 data were acquired using collision induced dissociation (CID) as activation type at 35% of collision energy (value optimised manually) at a resolution of 120000 at m/z 200. Untargeted mass isolation occurred in the Quad-rupole section and subsequent fragments detection were done in the Orbitrap section (level 2; MS2). Analysis time was 2 min (per sample), controlled using Xcalibur software (ThermoFischer Scientific). Data were acquired as automatic data dependent acquisition mode top scan using the 30 most intense precursors as priority; peaks selected three times were added to an exclusion list for 30 s. Each spectrum was exported as *.mzML files in order to be read by LipidXplorer (and as *.mzXML for the Molecular Network constructions) using the software msConvert (ProteoWizard; available at proteowizard.sourceforge.net/tools.shtml).

### LipidXplorer parameters

LipidXplorer 1.2.5 (32 bits) was used in this study. Data were imported as *.mzML files. Parameters for import were as follow: Selection window: 0.5 Da; Time range: 0–120 s; m/z range: 150–1500; Resolution: 560000 (140000 for MS2) at m/z 200; Tolerance: 10 ppm (20 ppm for MS2); Threshold: 100 (200 for MS2); Resolution gradient: −865 (−280 for MS2). Isotopic correction MS1 and MS2 was switched on for the identification process. The threshold parameter was adjusted to get the main signals as 1 × 103, directly from the acquired MS1 spectra.

MFQL files were written based on the structural formula for each group of compounds and their hydroxylated, methoxylated and glycosylated derivatives as described in the Supporting Information. Briefly, for each case, a skeleton with various degrees of O-substitution with hydroxy and methoxy groups, hexoses, pentoses and deoxyhexoses, from mono to tetrasaccharides, phenyl and phenylpropanoyl groups were considered. The parameters were chosen following recommendations from Herzog et al.6–8 MFQL files are available as Supporting Information online.

### MFQL descriptions

All MFQL files are available at the LipidXplorer wiki site at https://wiki.mpi-cbg.de/wiki/lipidx/index.php/Main_Page. Note that LipidXplorer can deliver quantitative results if the appropriate parameters and sample requirements are applied. Reliable quantification results require a validated internal standard, but such standards are difficult to obtain for natural products and therefore no quantification was done in this study. Details about creating the MFQL files are described in the Supporting Information.

### Labels and annotation

Labels present in each MFQL file for annotation purposes should represent the chemical class studied (Tables 2–4). Note that the structure type for each class with respect to its biosynthetic pathway and substituents were made as clear as ‘PHC6C3’ for caffeic acid derivative, ‘Monoglyc’ for derivatives with one additional sugar residue and methoxy substituents for derivatives with additional methoxy group (s) (Tables 2–4).

It should be noted that in most cases except for glycosylated derivatives, the additional carbon atom together with an additional oxygen atom and two hydrogens indicates the presence of a methoxy substituent (−OCH3) (Table 3). Only the common plant phenolics were considered; for more complex variations, new MFQL files would need to be written. C-methylations or C-glycosylations, since they are exceptional derivatives, were not considered in the MFQL queries written in this study; fragmentation (MS2) for C-glycoside derivatives are not considered here. In the case of flavonoids, an additional double bond will be identified to point out the occurrence of a flavone instead of a flavanone. Further details for the description of the MFQL files created here are available in the Supporting Information. An overview of a written MFQL file is presented (Figure 1).

In order to examine the specificity of our approach, a second set of MFQL queries were developed for ascarosides, a chemical group abundant in nematodes but not found in plants.19 Briefly, the MFQL files written for the ascarosides uses the information provided by von Reuss et al. 20 and for the characteristic neutral loss of m/z 130.0663 ([C6H10O3]). These restrictions were developed using the same basic structure described earlier but no specific labels were created for each class (Tables 5 and 6). The labels were defined on the basis of the structure classification provided by Figure 2. Then all the filters (phenolics and ascarosides) to all plant and nematode samples were applied.

### Test for efficiency of the restrictions

To test the efficiency of the restrictions proposed Compass MolWeight to Formula (Bruker Daltonik, Bremen, Germany) software was to determine the possible molecular formulae within 10 ppm of tolerance for some selected exact mass. The possible molecular formula for each m/z value was calculated with no restriction and added the number of carbon, oxygen and nitrogen atoms stepwise; those restrictions were extracted from the *.mfql files (Supporting Information).

### Script for automation of MFQL creation and visualisation of the results

To facilitate the writing of MFQL files an automated perl script called parse_cdxml.pl (available at https://github.com/rhilt13/MFQLAutomation) that can create these MFQL files from a more common type CDXML file from ChemOffice (Cambridgesoft) was designed; such a script creates only a MS1 type of query. This script allows the users to submit the parameters through a command line and also provide a *.cdxml file containing the molecules they are interested in. The script gets the information from the CDXML file inputs and formats it into a MFQL format. The result is a file ready to be used in LipidXplorer. With this script, automated generation of MFQL files could be performed more efficiently.

Once LipidXplorer is used, it produces a csv file that includes all the results. There are columns for masses, error, name of the precursors and fragments along with other information. A second perl script was designed, called get_struct.pl (available at https://github.com/rhilt13/MFQLAutomation) to parse those files, to pull structures for the previously listed precursors and fragments from CDXML files, perform calculations of the number of methoxy groups, hydroxy groups and double bonds that are present in each of the precursors and fragments, and compile all of this information into a textbox along with the structure into a.cdxml file. Automated extraction of the structure and related information improves analysis efficiency.

## RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Based on literature data and experimental fragmentation patterns of phenolics, MFQL files were written for the annotation of shikimic acid (C7), quinic acid (C7), benzoic acid (PhC6C1) and phenylpropanoid acid derivatives (PhC6C3), caffeoyl shikimic and dicaffeoyl shikimic acid derivatives (CSC6C3C7), caffeoyl quinic and dicaffeoyl quinic acid derivatives (CQC6C3C7), flavonoids (FlC6C3C6), and catechin derivatives (CatechC6C3C6). For example, PhC6C3 are known to exhibit neutral losses of 44 for CO2 from the side chain, and generally glycosylated derivatives exhibit neutral losses of 162, 146 and 132 for hexose, deoxyhexose and pentose, respectively.

All the molecular filtering tools were tested to survey a series of data dependent analysis (DDA) MS2 on selected samples of medicinal plants with well characterised composition. The same filters were applied to extracts from the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans to assess the specificity of the method. Detailed information on the generation the MFQL files are found in the Supporting Information and the terminology used is based on previously published LipidXplorer papers.6–8,20

All extracts and standards were analysed by DI-ESI-MS in negative ion mode under DDA mode to select the 30 most intense peaks for further fragmentation during 2 min of direct infusion. The acquired data yielded more than 350 MS2 spectra associated with up to 8400 features for a single extract.

The approach used in this study followed two steps. As a first step (step 1; Figure 3) the MS2 data were converted from proprietary into mzML format with MSConvert (Proteowizard) and then imported into LipidXplorer using the parameters described earlier. Those parameters were chosen based on the experimental data acquired. Secondly (step 2 Figure 3), MFQL files were firstly edited manually and written following expected molecular formula ranges and MS fragmentation patterns for each class and subclass of compounds. Subclasses were intended to be subdivisions of each class designed not to make the molecular formula range excessively broad, which would produce an incongruent number of false positive results. The details of step 2 are presented in the Supporting Information. Briefly, the MFQL file is separated into four sections: (1) Define; (2) Identify; (3) SuchThat; and (4) Report. In the Define section (line 6, Figure 1), a description of the expected molecular range, double bond ratio (DBR) and the mode of acquisition are made explicit for a given label that would represent the class/subclass of compound to be detected. In the Identify section (line 10, Figure 1), it is indicated where each defined label is to be found; MS1 for the survey spectra and MS2 for the fragmentograms. The SuchThat section (line 16, Figure 1) is a filter for false positive occurrences of the defined molecular ranges to be found; for example, for a flavonoid aglycone the number of additional carbon atoms should not the greater than the number of oxygen atoms since O-methylation only was considered and the representation of such a restriction is as follows: ‘pr2GlyFlC6C3C6OMe.chemsc [O] – 12 +2 >= pr2GlyFlC6C3C6OMe.chemsc [C] – 26’. The Report section (line 25, Figure 1) is where the output parameters are described; here one can print as much information as needed to aid in structure elucidation.

A characteristic flavonoid hesperidin (5,3’-dihydroxy-4’-methoxy-flavanone 7-O-rutinoside) was used as a known standard to verify the performances of the script. For this compound the MFQL files are expected to generate to classify it as a diglucosyl monomethoxy-dihydroxy-flavonoid; labelled as: “pr2GlyFlC6C3C6Me [n°C;DBR;n°O]”.

Using the assigned restriction only one molecular formula was found, C28H33O15. MS1 analysis generated the label “pr2GlyFlC6C3C6OMe[2:0:3]” in the output file which indicates three additional carbon atoms and two additional oxygen atoms from the basic structure of a diglycoside methoxy-flavonoid. The label for this flavonoid indicates 0 as the DBR number, excluding a flavone type of phenolic. The filtering thus indicates a diglycoside methoxy-flava-none with two additional carbon and three additional oxygen atoms. This combination indicates a number of possible structures for the detected signal at m/z 609.1823 (“pr2GlyFlC6C3C6OMe[2:0:3]”; molecular formula: C28H34O15) (Figure 4): (1) dipentoside trimethoxy-hydroxy-flavavone; (2) pentoside hexoside dimethoxy-hydroxy-flavanone; (3) dihexoside methoxy-hydroxy-flavanone; (4) hexoside pentoside methoxy-trihydroxy-flavanone; (5) dideoxyhexoside methoxy-trihydroxy-flavanone; (6) pentoside deoxyhexoside dimethoxy-dihydroxy-flavanone. It is impossible to identify the exact position of the hydroxy and the methoxy substituents and the nature of the glycosides on the aglycone using the data acquired by a simple direct infusion MS1 scan.

The MS2 analysis from the precursor ion at MS1 were then submitted to an additional MFQL file written based on common fragmentation patterns for phenolic compounds (Figure 4). When considering the fragments in MS2, the Define section (lines 7 and 8, Figure 1) of the MFQL file must have both entries for the precursor and for the diagnostic fragment and the Identify section must specify where in the MS file the specified restrictions will be queried as well (lines 12–14, Figure 1). For hesperidin the three main fragments were “pr1GlyFlC6C3C6OMe[1:0:3]” and “prFlC6C3C6OMe [0:0:2]” from the precursor “pr2GlyFlC6C3C6OMe[2:0:3]”. Considering the precursor at m/z 609.1823 “pr2GlyFlC6C3C6OMe[2:0:3]” and the fragments at m/z 463.1240 “pr1GlyFlC6C3C6OMe[1:0:3]” and at m/z 301.0720 “prFlC6C3C6OMe [0:0:2]” it is possible to understand that the first fragment is the neutral loss of 146 units, the second is the neutral loss of 162 units indicating the losses of a deoxyhexose and a hexose residue, respectively. The aglycone fragment at m/z 301.0720 (“prFlC6C3C6OMe [0:0:2]”) indicates two additional oxygen atoms and no additional carbon atom or DBR from fundamental structure of a trihydroxylated monomethoxylated-flavanone, since for this subclass glycosyl substituents are expected. Thus, the output data indicate that the aglycone fragment is a trihydoxy-methoxy-flavanone and the saccharide residues comprising of one deoxyhexose and one hexose (Figure 5). The position of the substituents cannot be ascertained but the information created is more restricted and might be sufficient for further screening studies.

The outcomes from direct MS1 and MS2 (level 1 and level 2) analysis can be compared. The complementary information obtained by MS2 analysis clearly enable to better define the type of flavonoid found, in this specific case one hexoside and one deoxyhexoside dihy-droxy-methoxyflavanone which correspond to the O-diglucosyl monomethoxy-dihydroxy-flavonoid expected.

Considering the full output generated MS1 analysis, there were 10 additional features in the sample accounting for less than 5% of the main signal of hesperidin at m/z 609.1823 (Figure 6). Those might represent impurities or even false positives. The same analysis done using the MS2 based MFQL file generated an output with three detected features. The signal at m/z 609.1823 (“pr2GlyFlC6C3C6OMe[2:0:3]”) identified as the target hesperidin, the signals at m/z 593.1510 (“pr2GlyFlC6C3C6OMe[1:1:3]”) and m/z 609.1460 might be flavonoid contaminants from the isolation of the standard or false positive detections. The analysis of this commercial flavonoid already shows the power of this method since several impurities could be related to phenolics (Figure 6).

### Proof of concept using real samples

To assess the annotation capabilities of this method for the metabolite profiling of phenolics in crude plant extract the polar extracts of leaves of medicinal plants with well-established composition were analysed by DI-ESI-MS and submitted to filtering by MFQL files. The analyses enable the annotation of many common phenolics. Shikimic acid (“prSC7 [0:0:0]”), quinic acid (“prQC7 [0:0:0]”), caffeoylquinic acid (“prCQC6C3C7 [0:0:2]”), dicaffeoylquinic acid (“pr2CQC6C3C7 [0:0:4]”), feruloylquinic acid (“prCQC6C3C7OMe [0:0:1]”), naringenin (“prFlC6C3C6 [0:0:3]”), quercetin (“prFlC6C3C6 [0:1:5]”), myricetin (“prFlC6C3C6 [0:1:6]”), mono and diglucosyl derivatives (“pr1GlyFlC6C3C6 (OMe) pr2GlyFlC6C3C6 (OMe)”) are among many of the identified compounds (Tables 7 and 8, also Supporting Information). Since the response is compound dependent it was not possible to mention which are the main ones. The outputs of these analyses are presented in the Supporting Information online due to the size of the tables.

To evaluate these results, this method was compared with the results obtained from MZmine, which is based on formal database queries, using the sample prepared from leaves of Coffea arabica. HMDB, Kegg compound database, LipidMaps database and PlantCyc database were used in online database searches and 10 ppm as “M/Z tolerance”. MZMine identified 69 compounds, from which 35 were nitrogen, phosphorus, chloride, fluoride and bromide free, 26 were phenolic derivatives and five were related to the classes for which this method was targeted (Figure 7). These last five compounds were: 3,4,5-trimethoxycinnamic acid, epicatechin, 3-O-p-coumaroylquinic acid, 3-O-feruloylquinic acid, 2-O-galloylsucrose and 1,3-dicaffeoylquinic acid; in addition to quinic acid. These five compounds were successfully detected by the LipidXplorer approach, together with more than 100 other compounds at a threshold of 0.1%.

In order to make a reasonable comparison between the identification capabilities from both the LipidXplorer approach and MZMine, additional MFQL files were written with MS1 information (using the script provided in Supporting Information) for the other 64 compounds identified by MZMine. Therefore, every compound identified by MZMine was detected. Thus, the method has the capability to match every identification done by the current software because it can be extended to cover all databases.

For the analysis of the coffee sample, the main phenolic constituents cited in the literature were identified:21–23 caffeoylquinic acid, feruloylquinic acid and dicaffeoylquinic acid derivatives (Table 7). Phenol-Explorer (database on polyphenol content in foods; http://phenol-explorer.eu) reports 16 phenolic compounds for coffee all related to caffeoylquinic acid derivatives. Additionally, the occurrence of shikimic and quinic acid, benzoic acid and glucosyl benzoic acid, caffeic acid and other shikimic acid derivatives were detected. Apart from some flavonoids detected, the presence of catechins (catechin, a catechin hexoside and a catechin pentoside) are highlighted.

Not to depend strictly on an experimental database has obvious advantages. To be able to classify unknown compounds represents a step forward in the discovery of new products. The output generated by LipidXplorer and our MFQL files could identify over 100 features and provide a self-designed label related to each structure for further identification (Supporting Information). For all samples studied here, LipidXplorer identified a broader range of compounds, due to its capability of survey for a range of substituent groups within a class.

Comparisons of literature data and MFQL queries for a commercial sample of green tea (Camellia sinensis) is provided12 (Table 8). Some of the flavonoid glycosides were not detected, but caffeoylquinic acid and catechin derivatives were found in the following forms: caffeoylquinic acid, epigallocatechin (“prCatechC6C3C6 [0:0:7]”), epicatechin (“prCatechC6C3C6 [0:0:6]”), gallocatechin (“prCatechC6C3C6 [0:0:7]”), catechin (“prCatechC6C3C6 [0:0:6]”), epigallocatechin gallate (“prCatechGalateC6C3C6 [0:5:8]”) and (epi-)cate-chin gallate (“prCatechGalateC6C3C6 [0:5:7]”). The absence of detectable signals of flavonoids might be due to seasoning, place of growth and/or ion suppression among other factors. Nonetheless, our approach enabled the detection of 39 compounds based on the phenolic’s targeted search with the MFQL queries.

In order to examine the specificity of our approach, a second set of MFQL files was developed for the unrelated ascarosides, a chemical group abundant in nematodes but not reported in plants. All the filters (phenolics and ascarosides) were applied to the plant and nematode samples. A heatmap of all plant samples against all Caenorhabditis elegans strains was used to compare the abundance of each class ranging the samples analysed within 5 ppm of mass error (Figure 8). Note the major occurrence of the ascarosides in the Caenorhabditis elegans strains rather than in plants. Some false positives can be found, probably due to isobaric compounds or even coincidental fragmentation patterns.

From the heatmap, it is possible to observe certain patterns such as the occurrence of shikimic acid in all plant samples, the high abundance of caffeoylquinic acid m/z features in the Coffea arabica samples and of hydroxy and methoxy flavones at the Echinacea spp., Glycyrrhiza glabra, Mimulus lewisii and M. cardinalis. The high ion intensities of methoxy flavonoids and monoglycoside derivatives in the Echinacea spp. is clear. From the data analysed here, it was not possible to correctly identify those false positive occurrences for the plant or the nematode samples. Signals at m/z 371, 387, 377 and 379 may be related to glucoside substituted jasmonic acid derivatives fairly common in plant leaves, and most of the other false positives might be related to alkyl sugar derivatives due to the loss of 162 and 180 units.

Hand annotation using the raw file spectra was done and compared to the output from LipidXplorer to corroborate the results. All of the semi-automatically-generated LipidXplorer results were identified as meaningful compounds. The most useful information to aid in such a validation was the “differenceFrag#” and “SUMCOMPOSITIONFrag#” parameters that yield the difference between the precursor and product ion masses. In most cases of positive results, this yielded the neutral loss of a hexose, pentose or a deoxyhexose, as expected. Thus, the effectiveness of this method will depend on how well the fragmentation pattern of different classes is described in the MFQL file. However, because fragmentation patterns can differ widely between different instruments, much deeper fragmentation might lead to false negative results. The user must consider carefully how detailed to describe the fragmentations at the MFQL file aiming to exclude the false positive results. Different instruments or even fine adjustments in the same instrument might give a slightly different fragmentation, mostly resulting in less intense signals.

The application of LipidXplorer was found to be successful to get a valuable qualitative snapshot of common phenolic contents within plant samples by applying the written MFQL files as restrictors. While direct infusion analysis can lose some information due to ion suppression, it has the great advantage of providing a fast screen, which is the main focus of this study. The output of our procedure simplifies dereplication of phenolic compounds from plants. All scripts are available in the Supporting Information or the Edison lab GitHub.

This method was evaluated against a well-used software (MZMine®) using well-known medicinal plants extracts. LipidXplorer was shown to be as useful to detect the presence of a compound regarding the MFQL file as MZMine that uses databases. Because our method is database-independent, it is better for possible new compound detection and classification. This simple generic method provides a complementary source of information for dereplication of natural products using MS2 based Molecular Networks.9,24,25 While being independent of databases, the presented detection filtering method for phenolics has the advantage to be generic and exchangeable between laboratories, an important aspect in natural products dereplication procedures.

Scripts were also created to aid in the generation of new MFQL files, which are relatively simple to create and apply to any class of natural products or metabolic pathways. This was illustrated here by the creation of a second set of MFQL files that is useful in analysis of ascarosides from nematodes. As other researchers develop and share similar MFQL files, dereplication and efficient annotation of natural products from the worldwide biodiversity will become easier. Even though LipidXplorer was designed for DI-ESI-MS data sets, it is possible to apply this approach for LC-MS/MS data using sequential values for the parameter “timerange” in the “Import Settings”.

# Metabolomics and Natural-Products Strategies to Study Chemical Ecology in Nematodes

**Authors:** Arthur S. Edison; Chaevien S. Clendinen; Ramadan Ajredini; Chris Beecher; Francesca V. Ponce; Gregory S. Stupp

**Affiliations:** *Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology and Southeast Center for Integrated Metabolomics, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL 32610-0245, USA; | †IROA Technologies, Ann Arbor, MI, USA; | ‡The Scripps Research Institute, Department of Molecular and Experimental Medicine, 10550 North Torrey Pines Road, La Jolla, CA 92037, USA

## Abstract

This review provides an overview of two complementary approaches to identify biologically active compounds for studies in chemical ecology. The first is activity-guided fractionation and the second is metabolomics, particularly focusing on a new liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry-based method called isotopic ratio outlier analysis. To illustrate examples using these approaches, we review recent experiments using Caenorhabditis elegans and related free-living nematodes.

## Introduction

This review focuses on a variety of analytical techniques and approaches that can be used to solve biological problems, especially those in chemical ecology and in behavior. As such, we will summarize some of the different technologies that are now available to characterize metabolites and low molecular weight signaling molecules. Each method has its own particular strengths and weaknesses, which we will emphasize by giving specific examples: research that we, and others, have done over the past decade on the model organism Caenorhabditis elegans and related nematodes. Even though it is best known as a model organism for genetics (Brenner 1974) and development (Sulston and Horvitz 1977), C. elegans is also an ideal animal for chemical studies (Schroeder 2006).

It is worth beginning with a brief discussion of two areas of chemical science that are particularly relevant to studies in ecology and behavior. The first is natural products chemistry, which typically starts with a complex mixture from an extract of an organism of interest, partially or fully purifies an active compound(s) using activity-guided fractionation (AGF), and identifies the active compound(s) using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and/or mass spectrometry (MS), which often is coupled to liquid or gas chromatography (LC or GC). The second is metabolomics, which typically starts with complex mixtures from two or more groups that differ by a specific phenotype of interest, collecting NMR or LC–MS/GC–MS data, and comparing the datasets statistically to identify biomarkers that show differences among the groups. The differences and similarities of natural products chemistry and metabolomics are summarized in Fig. 1, which was adapted from a recent review article comparing NMR-based natural products and metabolomics. The conclusion of that article is that the two fields are very closely related and, in fact, are merging in significant ways. Both start with complex mixtures of small-molecule metabolites, use the same analytical technologies, and have as a primary goal the identification of biologically active molecules or biomarkers (Robinette et al. 2012). Similar conclusions have been drawn using LC–MS (Constant and Beecher 1995; Wolfender et al. 2015). The plan of this review is as follows. The first section focuses on the use of AGF to target specific compounds of interest. This is a time-honored approach that is capable of leading to active compounds, even in low quantities. The drawback is that AGF is also time-consuming and only focuses on relatively few compounds. We then show how metabolomics can be used to obtain chemical information on a more global level, particularly focusing on a new LC–MS technique called isotopic ratio outlier analysis (IROA). We summarize several different approaches that are relevant to chemical ecology studies. Finally, we close with some ideas regarding strategies for integrating phenotypic data with natural products and metabolomics to gain new biological insight on a systems level.

## Activity-guided fractionation

AGF is conceptually simple and extremely useful as a method for discovering molecules with specific functions, but the necessary chromatography can be quite complex. The most important factor in AGF is the assay to measure the activity, which should be sensitive, easy, fast, and reproducible. These can be based on chemistry or biochemistry, such as enzymatic activity, or involve cells or organisms as detectors. A notable assay used male moths in cages as detectors in the purification of the active component of the mating pheromone, as reviewed by Hummel (1984). A more recent and high-tech assay used neuronal recordings of a moth’s antennal lobe combined with GC to identify complex odors associated with plant–pollinator relationships (Riffell et al. 2009). Interestingly, male elephants in a zoo were used to monitor the purification of males’ mating pheromone. We leave it to the imagination of the readers or to the original reference for a description of this purification (Rasmussen et al. 1997). As an evolutionary side-note, moths use the same mating pheromone as a component of their signaling system (Rasmussen et al. 1997).

We have used male C. elegans as detectors to purify the first mating pheromone in nematodes (Srinivasan et al. 2008). Details are provided in the primary reference, but the general procedure was to isolate large quantities of exudates from liquid cultures of C. elegans hermaphrodites and test these for male-specific responses using simple two-spot assays on agar plates, in which one spot has a buffer control and the other spot has a test fraction. We then monitor the time spent by males in each spot (Fig. 2). There are several important considerations when doing one of these assays. First, male and hermaphroditic worms respond to many things, including bacterial food. Therefore, bacteria must be separated from the worms to get a specific and meaningful response. We developed a “worm water” preparation, in which a synchronized population of hermaphrodites at a specific developmental stage was separated from bacteria using a sucrose gradient (Srinivasan et al. 2008; Kaplan et al. 2011; Choe et al. 2012). Then, the worms were allowed to sit in water or a defined buffer, and the supernatant was collected for bioassays. When purifying an unknown compound, it is important to develop a simple but accurate “accounting” system. Since by definition, we do not know what we are looking for before we find it, we can’t use molarity. When working with worms, we use our own units called “worm equivalents”, for which 1 worm equivalent is defined as the amount of material released by one worm in 1 h. Any convenient and consistent definition will suffice. Using this simple metric, it is easy to identify synergy or loss of activity or to detect other confounding factors.

We discovered after our initial study that male worms were able to respond to as little as 2.5 worm equivalents, which makes biological sense (Kaplan et al. 2011). It was also humbling to discover that our NMR spectrometer required about 4 million worm equivalents to detect the same pheromone (Fig. 3). This illustrates possibly the most important advantage of AGF over the metabolomics experiments described below: with a very sensitive bioassay like a male worm or moth, it is possible to detect the important components at concentrations that would be entirely missed with analytical instruments. One of the major complications of AGF is a synergetic effect of different metabolites responsible for the activity of the crude extract. In our study of the identification of males’ mating pheromone in C. elegans, we lost all activity at a key step in the fractionation (Srinivasan et al. 2008). The loss of activity could be caused by several factors, including degradation of the molecule(s), loss of the molecule(s) on the column, or synergy. Combining all the fractions and testing for activity, which will return if two or more compounds are acting synergistically, can rule out degradation or loss. With synergy, AGF gets more complicated. The evidence of synergy in that study is shown in Fig. 4b. Often a good start is to identify a fraction that is necessary but not sufficient for activity. This will yield at least one component, which can then be added to other fractions for additional bioassays.

In summary, AGF is a powerful but potentially very time-consuming way to identify biologically significant molecules. It can often reveal activity at concentrations that would be too low to measure with analytical instrumentation, and since it is always directed to the activity of interest, positive results will be relevant to the study. Synergy, compounds with masking or opposing activities, and bell-shaped responses can all complicate AGF. We have conducted two large AGF identifications of nematodes’ mating pheromones, and they both required several years of work to complete (Srinivasan et al. 2008; Choe et al. 2012); they are definitely not high-throughput!

## Metabolomic strategies

The right side of Fig. 1 summarizes a metabolomics approach to the identification of biomarkers. As illustrated, the end-point of a metabolomics and natural-products (AGF) study can be the same, but the mechanism and steps to get there are quite different. In metabolomics, the laborious step of AGF is eliminated. This can be wonderful news to anyone who has conducted an AGF study. There are some important differences in terms of overall design and outcomes of experiments between AGF and metabolomics.

The first is replicates of samples. Historically, AGF studies have not focused on obtaining large numbers of unique biological replicates, but in most cases many different samples need to be generated over the course of a study for subsequent steps in a purification scheme. In contrast, metabolomics is completely dependent upon statistical analysis. Therefore, a well-controlled design of the study, including appropriate numbers of replicates, is critical. It is always important in a metabolomics study to have discussions with an expert statistician.

Another important difference between AGF and metabolomics is the point at which analytical sensitivity becomes a major factor. Both approaches use the same types of MS and NMR instruments, but the reliance on the instruments is significantly different. In the example described above, male C. elegans were able to detect a pheromone produced by about 2.5 worm equivalents (Kaplan et al. 2011), while an outstanding NMR system (Brey et al. 2006) needed about 4 million worm equivalents of the same material. Based on knowledge gained from subsequent studies, we estimate that a sensitive LC–MS instrument would need about 10,000 worm equivalents for reliable detection of the same material (Stupp et al. 2013). The critical point here is that if we were relying entirely on NMR and MS instruments, as in the case in metabolomics, we would not find an active compound that is below our detection limits. However, with AGF, we know something of interest to the male worms is there, even if we need to produce a lot of material and concentrate it for NMR and MS. Thus, with metabolomics it is critical to always remember that the analytical instrumentation will define the number and concentrations of metabolites detected. Important biologically active compounds at concentrations too low to measure will be completely invisible in a metabolomics study.

One important distinction to make for metabolomics is “targeted” versus “untargeted” or “global” metabolomics. A full discussion of these is beyond the scope of this review, but excellent review articles have been published (Fiehn 2002; Dunn et al. 2011). In many ways, AGF could be considered a type of targeted metabolomics, for which the goal is to identify and quantify a specific compound based on activity. Targeted assays generally refer to classes such as “amino acids”, “organic acids”, but by using a biological detector like a male worm, a target class could also be “the group of compounds that causes males to be attracted”. Global metabolomics has several compelling advantages over targeted studies if an unbiased view of a given system (e.g., hypothesis-generation) is required. There are several different types of metabolomics experiments and general approaches to complex mixtures. We have recently reviewed and contrasted some of the methods used in NMR (Robinette et al. 2012). Here, we briefly describe a new metabolomics experiment that we think has some particular advantages for studies in chemical ecology.

As suggested above in the comparison of how many worm equivalents were needed to characterize a mating pheromone of C. elegans, NMR is less sensitive than MS. NMR typically requires about 100 nanomoles of material, but significant improvements with specialized technology can lower that to the just a few nanomoles (Dalisay et al. 2009; Molinski 2010; Ramaswamy et al. 2013). The major advantage of NMR is that it provides atom-specific information that is necessary for the full identification of an unknown molecule. NMR is also very reproducible, in part because the sample is in a tube that is not in contact with the instrument. Finally, NMR can be quantitative when the spectroscopist allows for full relaxation between scans. In contrast, MS is extremely sensitive, requiring much less material than NMR. For targeted analyses of known molecules, MS is generally much more efficient than NMR. On the other hand, LC–MS data can have many artifacts, and reproducibility is challenging, in part because the sample is in contact both with the chromatographic column and the detector in the MS instrument. MS data provide the mass/charge of each detected ion, and some instruments are capable tandem MS (MSn), which fragments ions that can be analyzed de novo or matched to databases for more definitive identification. Several reviews are available that expand on these basic introductory concepts (Katajamaa and Oresic 2007; Moco et al. 2007; Scalbert et al. 2009; Edison and Schroeder 2010; Wolfender et al. 2013).

## Isotopic ratio outlier analysis

IROA is a relatively new LC–MS-based experiment that we have used in experiments on metabolomics in C. elegans (Stupp et al. 2013). It has been reviewed (de Jong and Beecher 2012), so here we will focus on its utility for chemical ecology. In the basic IROA experiment, two different populations are compared, one that has been labeled with 5% 13C and the other with 95% 13C. 13C is a stable isotope that not only is useful for MS experiments but also is an excellent NMR nucleus, allowing for some combined analysis. The basic IROA workflow is shown in Fig. 5. There are several advantages of IROA for LC–MS metabolomics. First, the patterns of peaks created by the isotope labeling are easy to detect by a computer, greatly reducing artifacts. Second, the number of carbon atoms is known exactly for each MS peak, allowing for very efficient determination of molecular formulas. Finally, the relative quantities of the 5% and 95% channels are easily quantified. The result is that hundreds to thousands of peaks can be reliably detected and quantified. It is relatively easy to assign peaks to a molecular formula, but it is a greater challenge to figure out the true identity of all the peaks. There are many experiments that one could do with IROA. We will illustrate these with examples from nematodes, but virtually any system that can be labeled can be studied. For example, wild isolates of C. elegans, or other free-living species, could be collected and labeled with 5% 13C using labeled bacterial food. These could be compared with a common reference material of the laboratory wild-type (N2) strain that had been labeled with 95% 13C. With a very large batch of reference material, many different pairwise experiments can be conducted, and differences between wild isolates and N2 can be determined. These metabolic differences can then be compared with behavioral differences to correlate molecules or pathways with the phenotype. Another example would be to label a given strain with both 5% and 95% 13C and then add an unlabeled pathogen or other perturbation to the 5% channel. In this scenario, the global metabolic responses to the perturbation can be measured. Finally, in an experiment called “phenotypic IROA” (de Jong and Beecher 2012), the 5% 13C channel can be replaced by natural abundance 13C, which simply changes the pattern of isotopic distribution on the 12C side (blue peaks in Fig. 5). Some information is lost from the traditional IROA experiment, but with this it is possible to compare different species even if some cannot be cultured. For example, parasitic nematodes are notoriously difficult to culture, but one could compare these to a reference 95% 13C labeled C. elegans. It is important to note that in this situation, the experiment is more similar to a targeted study in which the targeted compounds are all labeled compounds from the reference strain, because they are the only ones that can be detected.

## Conclusion

We have attempted to illustrate different approaches that we have used to study chemical ecology in complex systems. The examples of nematodes follow from our own work and interests, but many different types of systems can be studied using similar experiments. There is no “perfect” approach, and in practice a combination of a natural products-based AGF and metabolomics is perhaps ideal. To find out the molecular basis of a specific behavior, a good starting point would be a simple and reliable bioassay for that behavior, followed by an AGF of the active compound(s). In parallel or sequentially, a metabolomics experiment could be developed to look more globally at the problem, either to avoid bias or to capture other compounds that may be relevant. A nice example of a combined approach is illustrated by the identification of both a male-specific and a female-specific mating pheromone in Panagrellus redivivus (Choe et al. 2012). In that study, the Edison and Sternberg laboratories conducted AGF on a mixed culture of worms and continued until gender-specific components were separated chromatographically. Two different ascarosides were discovered, ascr#1 that attracts males and dhas#18 that attracts females. Simultaneously, the Schroeder laboratory conducted a metabolomics-type experiment that used LC–MS to detect all ascarosides made by the species. They discovered ascr#1 and dhas#18, along with several other ascarosides not found in the AGF study. However, upon testing of the other ascarosides, none of them had significant activity in gender-specific attraction, suggesting other unknown functions (Choe et al. 2012). This study nicely illustrates the power both of natural products AGF and of metabolomics, which often can be used together to approach a question from two sides of the same coin (Robinette et al. 2012).
